summary: 36a analyzes the Mishna's description of the KG's bull: which tanna holds the bull stands between the vestibule and altar (R. Yehuda), and how the bull can simultaneously have its head pointing south and its face pointing west (its body runs east-west with head turned).

display.whats: Who holds that the bull stands 'between the vestibule and the altar'?
display.hint: Only R. Yehuda; the Rabbis place the confession at the east of the Azarah.
display.title: Whose View Places the Bull There?

learning.ahaMoment: The bull's location is a tannaic dispute: between vestibule and altar (R. Yehuda) vs east of the Azarah (Rabbis).
learning.memoryAnchor: Same bull, different location: R. Yehuda = vestibule-altar gap; Rabbis = eastern Azarah.
learning.learnerQuestion: The Mishna says the bull stands between the vestibule and the altar - but is that universally agreed?
learning.coreTension: The Mishna's stated location for the bull (between the vestibule and altar) needs an author, since the Rabbis are known to hold a different position.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara identifies R. Yehuda as the source of the Mishna's ruling, linking the confession's location to where the bull's blood is later sprinkled - the Rabbis place the confession further east in the Azarah.

takeaway.text: The Mishna's seemingly neutral description of the bull's location actually follows one specific tanna, R. Yehuda, whose view ties the confession site to the blood-sprinkling site.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners assume an unattributed Mishna reflects unanimous agreement; here it silently follows R. Yehuda against the Rabbis' dissenting view.

display.whats: How can the bull face both south (head) and west (face) simultaneously?
display.hint: The bull is turned sideways: body aligned east-west, head turned to face south.
display.title: Head South, Face West: How?

learning.ahaMoment: Bovine anatomy allows simultaneous orientations: body east-west, head turned south, face west.
learning.memoryAnchor: A sideways neck: bull's body east-west, head south, face west - KG east facing west, pressing on.
learning.learnerQuestion: How can the bull's head face south while its face simultaneously faces west?
learning.coreTension: The Mishna's description seems geometrically contradictory: the bull's head points south while its face points west.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara resolves this by orienting the bull's body along an east-west axis with its head turned sideways to the south, so the muzzle still points west - allowing the High Priest to stand east of the bull, facing west toward the Heichal, while pressing both hands on its head.

takeaway.text: An apparent contradiction in the Mishna's spatial description resolves once the turn of the bull's neck, not just its body axis, is accounted for.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners read 'head south' and 'face west' as describing two different parts of the body pointing in unrelated directions, rather than realizing both describe the same turned head.

rashiTranslations.en: Who do you hear hold that between the vestibule and the altar - is called north for the slaughter of the most
sacred offerings, from half the entrance of the Sanctuary and northward, between the vestibule and the altar, since we learned in the mishnah
that his bull stood between the vestibule and the altar, and we learned in the coming chapter (41b)
that he slaughtered it in the place of confession, as it teaches: he comes to his second bull and places his two hands
etc., slaughtered it and received it in a basin, etc. And opposite
the whole altar - thirty-two cubits,
opposite the altar to the north, is called north
for slaughtering the most sacred offerings; but what is not opposite
the altar, to the west or east side, even though
it is the north of the courtyard, it is not the north for slaughter,
since we require 'on the side of the altar,' as it is written
(Leviticus 1), 'and he shall slaughter it on the side of the altar,
northward.' Even between the vestibule and the altar - any
northern portion toward the west, even though it is not
literally the side; but the northern portion that is east
of the altar, no. Rebbi
adds - even all the north of the courtyard within the eleven
cubits of the area where the priests
tread, up to the eastern wall of the courtyard.
But from the beit hachalifot inward - the width
of the vestibule exceeds the width of the Sanctuary by fifteen
cubits to the north, and correspondingly to the south, and the length of that
excess is only ten cubits, from east
toward the west, and that excess is called
the beit hachalifot, which had twenty-four
windows, one window for each priestly watch, where they stored
the sacred knives, and a knife is called chalif
in Arabic; and the air behind that
excess toward the west, and the air between the north wall
of the excess and the wall of the courtyard, is called inward
from the beit hachalifot. All agree it is invalid -
since the altar is not visible there, it is not
called the side of the altar. Let us say - specifically
Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon holds this, and not
Rebbi. Now, Rebbi against Rabbi Yosei adds
etc. - meaning, what is your question? It is obvious
that they are not speaking precisely, and that Rebbi,
who adds the north of the eastern side, which is
further from the Sanctuary's own sanctity, adds it against Rabbi Yosei
specifically, but regarding Rabbi Elazar's own view he does not hold so; one could say that the further point
is valid and the closer point is invalid. We are saying this - meaning it is certainly obvious

to us that Rebbi too holds that between the vestibule and the altar is north, and this that the mishnah says 'let us say' it is not like Rebbi, this is our own difficulty, that the tanna of the mishnah does not hold like Rebbi

who validates the whole north of the courtyard, for if it were like Rebbi, why bring it close specifically to between the vestibule and the altar? Let him place it in any northern portion of the whole courtyard wherever he wishes.
Rather, what - Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon? Let him place it between the altar's own northern wall and the courtyard's northern wall, since according to everyone the essential 'side of the altar'
is truly there. Rather, what can you say - why does he bring it so close? Because of the priest's own weakness - so that the weight of the blood basin not be heavy upon him

from far away. For Rebbi too - even though the whole courtyard is valid in its own north, he brings it close to the entrance because of the priest's own weakness. Let us place it explicitly - his back to the altar
and his face to the Sanctuary. Lest he pass excrement - it is disgraceful to show the place of his waste toward the altar, and it is better this way, that his tail faces north and his head south,

so that his tail is not opposite the altar, since he does not draw it southward the whole length of the bull, but rather only part of his body is between the vestibule and the altar. How does one lean - all

leaning of the most sacred offerings. He stands in the north - since the most sacred offerings require north. And his face west - and his back east. And the one leaning - the owner. Stands in the east -

his back to the east. Sin of a sin-offering - that sin for which he brings it. And for a burnt-offering, the sin of gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner - since these have no confession of their own, this is how we read it in the Tosefta

of Menachot (chapter 10), and we do not read in it 'poor man's tithe,' since that one has its own confession, and also 'and I have given it to the Levite' - this is the first tithe, 'to the orphan and widow' - this is the poor man's tithe (Ma'aser Sheni, chapter 5,

mishnah 10). Rabbi Akiva says: a burnt-offering does not come, etc. - the reason is explained in the Tosefta: for what does a burnt-offering come? If for matters punishable by karet or court death, their punishment

is already stated; if for a negative commandment, its own punishment of lashes is stated. So a burnt-offering comes only for a positive commandment, or for a negative commandment convertible to a positive one, for which there is no lashing.
With a [negative commandment] - the daf ends mid-comment here; the comment (on which negative commandment their dispute concerns) continues on 36b.
